entry.title: Lean, formal proofs, and verifiable reasoning
entry.summary: An introduction to Lean, its mathematical history, and how formal proofs help us distinguish correct reasoning from plausible answers.
entry.content:
Lean is a programming language in which mathematical proofs can be checked by a computer. This post gives an introduction to Lean, from its origins and recent history to its applications to model reasoning and verifiable reinforcement learning.

What is Lean?​

Lean is a modern interactive theorem prover and functional programming language. It takes this dual nature seriously, and can be used meaningfully for both tasks.

Functional programming language. As a language, Lean is a strict, pure functional language with a dependent type theory. The latter property here is the most important to understand: it means that types in Lean can contain programs, and that programs can compute types. It is this powerful type system that enables Lean to "do mathematics".

# regular types - notice these only depend on other types
List Int
Prod String Bool

# dependent types
Vector Int 5        -- a list of length 5
Fin n               -- natural numbers less than n
Matrix m n ℝ        -- matrices indexed by m and n, with values in ℝ

Interactive theorem prover. Lean is expressive enough to do mathematics in a way that feels natural and idiomatic. For example, consider this definition and statement related to prime numbers:

/-- A prime is a number larger than 1 with no nontrivial divisors -/
def IsPrime (n : Nat) := 1 < n ∧ ∀ k, 1 < k → k < n → ¬ k ∣ n

/-- Every number larger than 1 has a prime factor -/
theorem exists_prime_factor :
    ∀ n, 1 < n → ∃ k, IsPrime k ∧ k ∣ n

A proof of the theorem exists_prime_factor is a term of that type. If one is able to produce such a term as validated by Lean's kernel, then one has proved the theorem!

Continuing this example
/-- A prime is a number larger than 1 with no nontrivial divisors -/
def IsPrime (n : Nat) := 1 < n ∧ ∀ k, 1 < k → k < n → ¬ k ∣ n

/-- Every number larger than 1 has a prime factor -/
theorem exists_prime_factor :
    ∀ n, 1 < n → ∃ k, IsPrime k ∧ k ∣ n := by
  intro n h1
  -- Either `n` is prime...
  by_cases h_prime : IsPrime n
  · grind [Nat.dvd_refl]
  -- ... or it has a non-trivial divisor with a prime factor
  · obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ : ∃ k, 1 < k ∧ k < n ∧ k ∣ n := by
      simp_all [IsPrime]
    obtain ⟨p, hp, hpk⟩ := exists_prime_factor k (by grind)
    grind [Nat.dvd_trans]

/-- The factorial, defined recursively, with custom notation -/
def factorial : Nat → Nat
  | 0 => 1
  | n+1 => (n + 1) * factorial n
notation:10000 n "!" => factorial n

/-- The factorial is always positive -/
theorem factorial_pos : ∀ n, 0 < n ! := by
  intro n; induction n <;>
    grind [factorial, Nat.mul_pos_iff_of_pos_left]

/-- ... and divisible by its constituent factors -/
theorem dvd_factorial : ∀ n, ∀ k ≤ n, 0 < k → k ∣ n ! := by
  intro n; induction n <;>
    grind [Nat.dvd_mul_right, Nat.dvd_mul_left_of_dvd, factorial]

/--
We show that we find arbitrarily large (and thus infinitely
many) prime numbers, by picking an arbitrary number `n`
and showing that `n! + 1` has a prime factor larger than `n`.
-/
theorem InfinitudeOfPrimes : ∀ n, ∃ p > n, IsPrime p := by
  intro n
  have : 1 < n ! + 1 := by grind [factorial_pos]
  obtain ⟨p, hp, _⟩ := exists_prime_factor (n ! + 1) this
  suffices ¬p ≤ n by grind
  intro (_ : p ≤ n)
  have : 1 < p := hp.1
  have : p ∣ n ! := dvd_factorial n p ‹p ≤ n› (by grind)
  have := Nat.dvd_sub ‹p ∣ n ! + 1› ‹p ∣ n !›
  grind [Nat.add_sub_cancel_left, Nat.dvd_one]

Dual nature of Lean. The way to connect these concepts is as follows. Theorems in Lean (or mathematical statements in general) are thought of as types, and a proof of a theorem corresponds to an instance of that type.

# as a programming language
n : Int := 73

# as a theorem prover
theorem exists_prime_factor : ∀ n, 1 < n → ∃ k, IsPrime k ∧ k ∣ n := by intro n h1 ...

This simple example already speaks to the potential of Lean as a way to verify statements of mathematics (and by extension, of reasoning) through a compiler. Before going any deeper however, let's start with a bit of historical context.

A brief history​

Origins of Lean at Microsoft Research.

Lean was created by Leonardo de Moura at Microsoft Research (MSR) in 2013 with the goal of building a next-generation theorem prover. By 2017, Lean 3 was released, which became the first mature and widely adopted version.

Lean enters pure mathematics - AKA the Buzzard effect.

In 2019, Kevin Buzzard gives a talk at Microsoft on the Future of Mathematics arguing that Lean will become an essential tool for working mathematicians. This catalyzes a cultural shift in the mathematics community, exemplified by figures like Peter Scholze and Terry Tao (both winners of the Fields Medal) adopting Lean.

There are two important questions answered in this period:

  1. Is Lean broad enough to cover the full spectrum of mathematics - from algebra to number theory, from statistics to theoretical physics?
  2. Is Lean powerful enough to express the deepest areas of mathematics - including the latest research? One might fear that as you approach the frontiers of mathematics research, the objects themselves become prohibitively expensive to formalize.

There is strong evidence supporting positive answers to both questions, which we now go over.

On the question of breadth.

  • Formalizing the undergraduate curriculum at Imperial College London: In 2021, Kevin Buzzard started to systematically formalize the pure mathematics curriculum at Imperial College. This program covers topics from algebra, number theory, measure theory, topology, graph theory, Galois theory and commutative algebra (repo, blog post).
  • Mathlib is the unified mathematics library for Lean. Created in 2017, by November 2025 it contained roughly 1.9 million lines of code, over 240k theorems, and over 100k definitions, covering an incredibly broad range of subjects. You can see its growth statistics here. Check out these papers from 2019 and 2025 for more details.

Lean demonstrates research-level capability.

In 2020 Peter Scholze (Fields Medalist) announces the Liquid Tensor Experiment with the goal to formalize a difficult foundational theorem from his work on analytic geometry. Here is the technical statement they aimed to formalize:

Theorem [Clausen-Scholze]. Let 0<p0<p≤10 < p_0 < p \le 10<p0​<p≤1 be real numbers, let SSS be a profinite set, and let VVV be a ppp-Banach space. Let Mp0(S)M_{p_0}(S)Mp0​​(S) be the space of p0p_0p0​-measures on SSS. Then

Ext⁡Cond⁡(Ab)i(Mp0(S), V)=0\operatorname{Ext}^i_{\operatorname{Cond}(\mathbf{Ab})} \bigl( M_{p_0}(S),\, V \bigr) = 0ExtCond(Ab)i​(Mp0​​(S),V)=0

for all i≥1i \ge 1i≥1.

This is an important example because both the objects being discussed and the theorem itself are highly complex (it requires years of training to even understand the basic definitions). To quote Kevin Buzzard:

Hales and Gonthier have already demonstrated beyond all doubt that it is possible to prove highly complex theorems about relatively low-level objects (spheres, finite groups, planar graphs) in a theorem prover. This is the next step - can we prove a complex theorem about a complex object?

Around six months later, the key result in the challenge was formalized, and a year later the entire challenge was completed. Here's a quote from Peter Scholze's blog post announcing the result:

I am excited to announce that the Experiment has verified the entire part of the argument that I was unsure about. I find it absolutely insane that interactive proof assistants are now at the level that within a very reasonable time span they can formally verify difficult original research. Congratulations to everyone involved in the formalization!!

There's a lot more one can say about this experiment! For the curious:

  • Scholze's challenge in full.
  • Buzzard's Beyond Liquid Tensor Experiment blog post.
  • An interactive visualization of the completed proof.

TL;DR: Lean can formalize deep mathematics.

Mathematics community.

Lean has become a prominent tool within the mathematics community. Figures like Terry Tao are writing about formalization and discussing Lean in talks. Ambitious projects like the Fermat's Last Theorem formalization project (Buzzard et al., estimated to take more than ten years to complete) are receiving grants.

DeepMind reaches silver-medal standard at the IMO (2024).

The machine learning community has taken notice of Lean too, with so-called neural theorem provers gaining popularity. In 2024, DeepMind achieved silver-medal-level performance on IMO problems. Here's an example problem that AlphaProof was able to solve.

IMO 2024 (Problem 2). Determine all pairs (a,b)(a, b)(a,b) of positive integers for which there exist positive integers ggg and NNN such that

gcd⁡(an+b,bn+a)=g\gcd(a^n + b, b^n + a) = ggcd(an+b,bn+a)=g

holds for all integers n≥Nn \geq Nn≥N.

This can be formalized in Lean as follows.

theorem imo_2024_p2 :
    {(a, b) |  0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧
      ∃ g N, 0 < g ∧ 0 < N ∧
        ∀ n ≥ N, Nat.gcd (a ^ n + b) (b ^ n + a) = g} = {(1, 1)} :=

Remark. Notice that the original question is to find all pairs. Here, that task is expressed as a statement that the set of solutions is exactly {(1,1)}\{(1, 1)\}{(1,1)}. Finding the candidate solution and proving that it is complete are separate parts of the task.

Here is the original proof produced by AlphaProof:

AlphaProof full solution to IMO 2024 (Problem 2)
refine Set.eq_singleton_iff_unique_mem.mpr ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · simp only [Set.mem_setOf]
    use one_pos; use one_pos
    use 2; use 1
    use two_pos; use one_pos
    rintro n -
    simp only [one_pow]
    exact Nat.gcd_self 2

  rintro ⟨a, b⟩
  rintro ⟨a_pos, b_pos, g, N, -, -, D⟩

  have a_coprime : a.Coprime (1 + a * b) := by
    rw [Nat.coprime_add_mul_left_right]
    exact Nat.coprime_one_right _
  have b_coprime : b.Coprime (1 + a * b) := by
    rw [Nat.coprime_add_mul_right_right]
    exact Nat.coprime_one_right _

  have a_euler := Nat.ModEq.pow_totient a_coprime
  have b_euler := Nat.ModEq.pow_totient b_coprime
  rw [←ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff] at a_euler b_euler

  have totient_pos :=
    ((1 + a*b).totient_pos).mpr ((zero_le _).trans_lt (lt_one_add _))

  suffices h : 1 + a * b ∣ g
  · specialize D (φ (1+a*b)*N) (Nat.le_mul_of_pos_left N totient_pos)
    have ⟨Ha, Hb⟩ :=
      D ▸ Nat.gcd_dvd (a ^ (φ (1 + a * b) * N) + b) (b ^ (φ (1 + a * b) * N) + a)
    replace Ha := h.trans Ha; replace Hb := h.trans Hb
    clear g D a_coprime b_coprime totient_pos h
    rw [←ZMod.natCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd, pow_mul] at Ha Hb
    push_cast at a_euler b_euler Ha Hb
    rw [a_euler] at Ha; clear a_euler
    rw [b_euler] at Hb; clear b_euler
    rw [one_pow] at Ha Hb
    norm_cast at Ha Hb
    rw [ZMod.natCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd] at Ha Hb
    replace Ha := Nat.le_of_dvd (Nat.add_pos_right 1 b_pos) Ha
    replace Hb := Nat.le_of_dvd (Nat.add_pos_right 1 a_pos) Hb
    rw [Prod.mk.injEq]
    constructor <;> nlinarith only [a_pos, b_pos, Ha, Hb]

  suffices h : ∃ n ≥ N, 1 + a * b ∣ a * (a ^ n + b) ∧
                        1 + a * b ∣ b * (b ^ n + a)
  · obtain ⟨n, hn, h⟩ := h
    replace h := And.intro
      (Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left a_coprime.symm h.1)
      (Nat.Coprime.dvd_of_dvd_mul_left b_coprime.symm h.2)
    replace h := Nat.dvd_gcd h.1 h.2
    rw [D _ hn] at h
    exact h
  clear D g a_coprime b_coprime a_pos b_pos

  use φ (1 + a * b) * (N + 1) - 1
  use N.le_sub_of_add_le (Nat.le_mul_of_pos_left (N + 1) totient_pos)

  obtain ⟨w, h : _ = w + 1⟩ := Nat.exists_eq_add_of_le' totient_pos
  clear totient_pos
  simp only [←ZMod.natCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd, pow_add]
  push_cast at a_euler b_euler ⊢
  rw [h] at a_euler b_euler ⊢; clear h
  constructor <;>
  simp only [mul_add, ←pow_succ', mul_one, Nat.add_succ_sub_one] <;>
  rw [add_assoc, ←mul_add_one] <;>
  rw [pow_mul] <;>
  simp only [a_euler, b_euler] <;>
  clear a_euler b_euler <;>
  simp only [one_pow] <;>
  norm_cast <;>
  simp only [ZMod.natCast_zmod_eq_zero_iff_dvd] <;>
  ring_nf <;>
  exact dvd_refl _

In 2025, both DeepMind and OpenAI reported gold-medal-level IMO performance, each solving five of the six problems. Unlike AlphaProof's 2024 results, these solutions were written in natural language rather than Lean.

Proofs in Lean​

At this point we can touch on the core mechanics of actually doing mathematics in Lean. Recall that a theorem in Lean is a type, and a proof is obtained by constructing an expression of that type.

Tactics​

There are multiple ways to do this in Lean, but the way that most closely resembles mathematics (and thus the most common approach in places like Mathlib) is called a tactic proof. Tactic proofs begin with the keyword by and proceed by applying a sequence of tactics. A tactic is a meta-program that helps automatically construct expressions of the desired type.

Here are some basic examples to give the idea.

TacticPurpose and example
rfl

Closes a goal when the two sides of an equality are definitionally equal.

example : 1 = 1 := by
  rfl
rw

rw [e] applies identity e as a rewrite rule to the target of the main goal.

example (a b : ℕ) (h : a = b) :
    a + 1 = b + 1 := by
  rw [h]
exact

exact e closes the main goal if its target type matches that of e.

example (a : ℕ) : a + 0 = a := by
  exact Nat.add_zero a
apply

apply e tries to match the current goal against the conclusion of e's type.

example (p q : Prop) (h_p : p)
    (h_pq : p → q) : q := by
  -- we need to show q
  -- apply the hypothesis h_pq,
  -- so now we need to show p
  apply h_pq
  -- but we have p, it's exactly
  -- the hypothesis h_p!
  exact h_p
linarith

A powerful tactic that solves linear inequalities of various kinds.

example : (0 : ℝ) ≤ 73 := by
  linarith
induction'

induction' n with d hd starts a proof by induction. Here hd becomes the induction hypothesis - i.e., we assume the statement holds for n = d and need to prove it holds for n = d + 1.

example (a : ℕ) : a + 1 = 1 + a := by
  -- begin a proof by induction
  induction' a with d hd
  -- case a = 0 amounts to proving 1 = 1
  · rfl
  -- case a = d, the inductive step
  · linarith
simp

Uses lemmas and hypotheses to simplify the main goal target or non-dependent hypotheses.

example (a b c d : ℕ) :
    (a + 0) * 1 + (b * 0 + c) +
      (d + 0) * 1 = a + c + d := by
  simp

Tactics allow us to approach proving statements in Lean in a similar way to proving statements in mathematics. In either setting, one structures their argument as a series of steps until the final goal has been obtained. Tactics are a powerful concept as they let you construct programs to write proofs interactively, procedurally and even automatically, as we will see.

The proof state​

Tactics, it turns out, are only half the story when writing proofs in Lean. The other half is the proof state. This is a representation of the current goal you are trying to prove, together with all the local context you have (like hypotheses that are given, or that you have established along the way).

Lean reports the current proof state in the Lean Infoview window (powered by the Lean LSP in tools like VS Code, for example). A typical view might look something like this:

1 goal
n : ℕ
hn : 1 < n
⊢ ∃ k, IsPrime k ∧ k ∣ n

This can be read as follows:

  • There is currently 1 goal, that is, one thing we need to prove.
  • We have a natural number n : ℕ and a hypothesis hn : 1 < n that nnn is greater than 1.
  • The thing we need to prove is after the ⊢ symbol. In this case we need to prove the existence of a number kkk that divides nnn and that is prime.

As you apply tactics, you modify the proof state. You might do this by adding new variables or hypotheses, by rewriting or adjusting the remaining goal, by splitting the existing goal into subgoals, and so forth.

David Renshaw's chess analogy​

David Renshaw draws the following analogy between chess and Lean.

Chess. You can write down a chess game as a sequence of moves in algebraic notation, but this leaves implicit the main visual element of chess: the position of the pieces on the board. For example, here's a representation of the Game of the Century.

1.Nf3 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.d4 O-O 5.Bf4 d5 6.Qb3 dxc4
7.Qxc4 c6 8.e4 Nbd7 9.Rd1 Nb6 10.Qc5 Bg4 11.Bg5 Na4
12.Qa3 Nxc3 13.bxc3 Nxe4 14.Bxe7 Qb6 15.Bc4 Nxc3
16.Bc5 Rfe8+ 17.Kf1 Be6 18.Bxb6 Bxc4+ 19.Kg1 Ne2+
20.Kf1 Nxd4+ 21.Kg1 Ne2+ 22.Kf1 Nc3+ 23.Kg1 axb6
24.Qb4 Ra4 25.Qxb6 Nxd1 26.h3 Rxa2 27.Kh2 Nxf2
28.Re1 Rxe1 29.Qd8+ Bf8 30.Nxe1 Bd5 31.Nf3 Ne4
32.Qb8 b5 33.h4 h5 34.Ne5 Kg7 35.Kg1 Bc5+ 36.Kf1 Ng3+
37.Ke1 Bb4+ 38.Kd1 Bb3+ 39.Kc1 Ne2+ 40.Kb1 Nc3+
41.Kc1 Rc2# 0-1

When we play chess we want to see the board as a way to help reason over the game state.

Lean. You can write a proof in the Lean theorem prover as a sequence of steps, but this format leaves implicit the main visual element of theorem proving: the goal state. For example, here's the statement about prime factors from earlier:

theorem exists_prime_factor :
    ∀ n, 1 < n → ∃ k, IsPrime k ∧ k ∣ n

When we use Lean we want to see the goal we are trying to prove. Lean provides this information, and we can watch it evolve as we make steps in the proof. The walkthrough below follows the complete proof, from the initial goal to both cases being closed.

Mathlib, and the growing repository of results​

As mentioned above, Mathlib is an extensive library of definitions and theorems. As of November 2025, Mathlib had over 240k theorems and over 100k definitions. Lean supports importing and using existing results to help prove theorems. One simply needs to import the relevant module, e.g., import Mathlib.Algebra.Polynomial.Basic.

Tactics and automation​

Beyond the existence of a large repository of known results, Lean has various kinds of automation built in to assist the working mathematician.

Example: Rewrite suggestion. In Lean there is a rewrite move denoted rw which applies a fact to the current proof state to modify the goal. One can interact with Lean by asking rw? (with a question mark) to get suggestions based on your active state!

import Mathlib

example (a b c : Nat) : a * b * c = b * (a * c) :=
by
  rw?

Possible rewrite suggestions from Mathlib include:

Try this: rw [Nat.mul_right_comm]
-- a * c * b = b * (a * c)
Try this: rw [Nat.mul_assoc]
-- a * (b * c) = b * (a * c)
Try this: rw [Nat.mul_left_comm]
-- a * b * c = a * (b * c)
Try this: rw [Nat.mul_comm]
-- c * (a * b) = b * (a * c)
Try this: rw [← Nat.mul_assoc]
-- a * b * c = b * a * c

What's the difference between formal and informal reasoning, and why should you care?​

Consider the following example question from AMC-12:

Let x,y∈Rx, y \in \mathbb{R}x,y∈R satisfy ∣x+y∣+∣x−y∣=2|x + y| + |x-y| = 2∣x+y∣+∣x−y∣=2. Show that

x2−6x+y2≤8x^2 - 6x + y^2 \leq 8x2−6x+y2≤8

Here's an excerpt from GPT-5's attempt at solving this problem:

The constraint ∣x+y∣+∣x−y∣=2|x+y|+|x-y|=2∣x+y∣+∣x−y∣=2 is the boundary of a diamond (a square rotated 45∘45^\circ45∘) with vertices (±1,±1)(\pm1,\pm1)(±1,±1).

We want to maximize

f(x,y)=x2−6x+y2=(x−3)2+y2−9.f(x,y)=x^2-6x+y^2=(x-3)^2+y^2-9.f(x,y)=x2−6x+y2=(x−3)2+y2−9.

So maximizing fff is the same as maximizing the squared distance from (3,0)(3,0)(3,0):

(x−3)2+y2.(x-3)^2+y^2.(x−3)2+y2.

On that diamond, the farthest points from (3,0)(3,0)(3,0) are the left vertices (−1,1)(-1,1)(−1,1) and (−1,−1)(-1,-1)(−1,−1). (Geometrically: draw the diamond and the point (3,0)(3,0)(3,0); the farthest boundary points are the two left corners.)

Evaluate:

  • f(−1,1)=(−1)2−6(−1)+12=1+6+1=8f(-1,1)=(-1)^2-6(-1)+1^2=1+6+1=8f(−1,1)=(−1)2−6(−1)+12=1+6+1=8.
  • f(−1,−1)=1+6+1=8f(-1,-1)=1+6+1=8f(−1,−1)=1+6+1=8.
  • For comparison, the right vertices give f(1,±1)=1−6+1=−4f(1,\pm1)=1-6+1=-4f(1,±1)=1−6+1=−4.

Answer

  • Maximum value: (8)
  • Where: at (−1,1) and (−1,−1)\boxed{(-1,1)\ \text{and}\ (-1,-1)}(−1,1) and (−1,−1)​

Notice:

  • GPT-5 makes a geometric argument based on the shape determined by the given constraint.
  • Its description is inconsistent: the vertices (±1,±1)(\pm1,\pm1)(±1,±1) define an axis-aligned square, not a square rotated by 45 degrees.
  • It gives no justification for identifying the constraint with that boundary.
  • Completing the square correctly reduces the problem to maximizing the distance from (3,0)(3,0)(3,0).
  • The final maximizing points are correct, but the geometric explanation is muddled. A correct answer alone does not establish that the reasoning is sound.

Here's a picture of the region enclosed by the constraint in the problem (shaded in green). The constraint itself is the boundary of that region. Looking at this, it's possible to guess at the reason the model mentioned diamonds rotated by 45 degrees.

Question: how much credit should be assigned to this answer? It has the right flavor, and indeed makes many of the correct steps. But it leaves a gap between a plausible explanation and a justified argument. Worse, that gap is not obvious at a glance! This makes an LLM-as-a-judge-based reward hard to trust.

Consider now the formal version of this problem:

example
  (x y : ℝ)
  (h₀ : abs (x + y) + abs (x - y) = 2) : x ^ 2 - 6 * x + y ^ 2 ≤ 8

Notice that it is straightforward to give the formal version of this problem in Lean.

The advantage of formalization is that the proof can be checked against a precise statement, rather than relying on a fallible LLM-as-a-judge. We still need to ensure that the formal statement matches the intended problem, that the proof has no gaps, and that it uses only permitted axioms.

Here is a model-generated formal solution. Before expanding the argument, here are some key observations:

  • This argument was model-generated, showing that models are capable of detailed Lean-based proofs.
  • The proof is over 80 lines long. There is some tax to pay for being precise in one's argument.
  • If you are not familiar with Lean, the argument may be tricky to follow. But remember, Lean is just a programming language (admittedly with a fairly steep learning curve).
Full Lean proof
 by
  by_cases hxy : x + y ≥ 0
  · by_cases hxx : x - y ≥ 0
    · have hx : x = 1 := by
        rw [abs_of_nonneg hxy, abs_of_nonneg hxx] at h₀
        linarith
      have hy_le : y ≤ 1 := by linarith [hx, hxx]
      have hy_ge : y ≥ -1 := by linarith [hx, hxy]
      have hy_abs : abs y ≤ 1 := by
        apply abs_le.mpr
        exact ⟨hy_ge, hy_le⟩
      have hy_tmp : (abs y) ^ 2 ≤ abs y := by
        rw [pow_two]
        apply mul_le_of_le_one_right
        · simp
        · exact hy_abs
      have hy_sq : y ^ 2 ≤ 1 := by
        simpa [sq_abs] using le_trans hy_tmp hy_abs
      calc
        x ^ 2 - 6 * x + y ^ 2 = 1 - 6 + y ^ 2 := by simp [hx]
        _ = y ^ 2 - 5 := by ring
        _ ≤ 1 - 5 := by linarith [hy_sq]
        _ = -4 := by norm_num
        _ ≤ 8 := by linarith
    · have hy : y = 1 := by
        rw [abs_of_nonneg hxy, abs_of_nonpos (le_of_not_ge hxx)] at h₀
        linarith
      have hx_le : x ≤ 1 := by linarith [hy, hxx]
      have hx_ge : x ≥ -1 := by linarith [hy, hxy]
      have hx_abs : abs x ≤ 1 := by
        apply abs_le.mpr
        exact ⟨hx_ge, hx_le⟩
      have hx_tmp : (abs x) ^ 2 ≤ abs x := by
        rw [pow_two]
        apply mul_le_of_le_one_right
        · simp
        · exact hx_abs
      have hx_sq : x ^ 2 ≤ 1 := by
        simpa [sq_abs] using le_trans hx_tmp hx_abs
      have h_lin : -6 * x ≤ 6 := by
        linarith [hx_ge]
      calc
        x ^ 2 - 6 * x + y ^ 2 = x ^ 2 - 6 * x + 1 := by simp [hy]
        _ ≤ 1 + 6 + 1 := by linarith [hx_sq, h_lin]
        _ = 8 := by norm_num
  · by_cases hxx : x - y ≥ 0
    · have hy : y = -1 := by
        rw [abs_of_nonpos (le_of_not_ge hxy), abs_of_nonneg hxx] at h₀
        linarith
      have hx_ge : x ≥ -1 := by linarith [hy, hxx]
      have hx_le : x ≤ 1 := by linarith [hy, hxy]
      have hx_abs : abs x ≤ 1 := by
        apply abs_le.mpr
        exact ⟨hx_ge, hx_le⟩
      have hx_tmp : (abs x) ^ 2 ≤ abs x := by
        rw [pow_two]
        apply mul_le_of_le_one_right
        · simp
        · exact hx_abs
      have hx_sq : x ^ 2 ≤ 1 := by
        simpa [sq_abs] using le_trans hx_tmp hx_abs
      have h_lin : -6 * x ≤ 6 := by
        linarith [hx_ge]
      calc
        x ^ 2 - 6 * x + y ^ 2 = x ^ 2 - 6 * x + 1 := by simp [hy]
        _ ≤ 1 + 6 + 1 := by linarith [hx_sq, h_lin]
        _ = 8 := by norm_num
    · have hx : x = -1 := by
        rw [abs_of_nonpos (le_of_not_ge hxy), abs_of_nonpos (le_of_not_ge hxx)] at h₀
        linarith
      have hy_le : y ≤ 1 := by linarith [hx, hxy]
      have hy_ge : y ≥ -1 := by linarith [hx, hxx]
      have hy_abs : abs y ≤ 1 := by
        apply abs_le.mpr
        exact ⟨hy_ge, hy_le⟩
      have hy_tmp : (abs y) ^ 2 ≤ abs y := by
        rw [pow_two]
        apply mul_le_of_le_one_right
        · simp
        · exact hy_abs
      have hy_sq : y ^ 2 ≤ 1 := by
        simpa [sq_abs] using le_trans hy_tmp hy_abs
      calc
        x ^ 2 - 6 * x + y ^ 2 = 1 + 6 + y ^ 2 := by simp [hx]
        _ = 7 + y ^ 2 := by norm_num
        _ ≤ 7 + 1 := by linarith [hy_sq]
        _ = 8 := by norm_num

Takeaways.

This example highlights fundamental challenges with informal reasoning-based methods stemming from the difficulty with scalably identifying flawed reasoning trajectories, particularly in cases where the flaws are subtle. We see how formally verifiable solutions provide a remedy.

entry.title: Composition factors and representation stability
entry.summary: Computing Schur-functor multiplicities by decomposition puzzles and shape analysis, and the representation stability revealed by the resulting coefficients.
entry.content:
In 2017, my advisor asked me to compute a family of coefficients cλμc_{\lambda\mu}cλμ​ arising in the study of the Johnson homomorphism of the mapping class group.

Their connection with mapping class groups is not essential to this story. Instead, I want to describe how to compute them efficiently, and how expanding the range of computation revealed hints of a deeper structure among the coefficients.1

Plethysms afoot​

So, briefly, what are the coefficients cλμc_{\lambda\mu}cλμ​?

Recall that, given a partition λ⊢n\lambda\vdash nλ⊢n, the Schur functor Sλ\mathbb S_\lambdaSλ​ assigns to a vector space VVV the image of a Young symmetrizer acting on V⊗nV^{\otimes n}V⊗n. Two familiar examples are the symmetric powers S(n)(V)=Sym⁡n(V)\mathbb S_{(n)}(V)=\operatorname{Sym}^n(V)S(n)​(V)=Symn(V) and exterior powers S(1n)(V)=⋀nV\mathbb S_{(1^n)}(V)=\bigwedge^n VS(1n)​(V)=⋀nV.

The free Lie algebra L(V)\mathcal L(V)L(V) is the Lie algebra generated by VVV, subject only to antisymmetry and the Jacobi identity. It has a natural grading

L(V)=⨁n≥1Ln(V),\mathcal L(V)=\bigoplus_{n\geq 1}\mathcal L_n(V),L(V)=n≥1⨁​Ln​(V),

where Ln(V)\mathcal L_n(V)Ln​(V) consists of Lie expressions involving exactly nnn inputs from VVV.

We are interested in the coefficients cλμc_{\lambda\mu}cλμ​ defined by the decomposition

Sμ(L(V))≅⨁λSλ(V)⊕cλμ.\mathbb S_\mu\bigl(\mathcal L(V)\bigr) \cong \bigoplus_\lambda \mathbb S_\lambda(V)^{\oplus c_{\lambda\mu}}.Sμ​(L(V))≅λ⨁​Sλ​(V)⊕cλμ​.

In other words, cλμc_{\lambda\mu}cλμ​ is the multiplicity of Sλ(V)\mathbb S_\lambda(V)Sλ​(V) in Sμ(L(V))\mathbb S_\mu(\mathcal L(V))Sμ​(L(V)).2

How might we compute these coefficients?

The first observation is that the graded pieces of the free Lie algebra themselves admit Schur-functor decompositions:

Ln(V)≅⨁ν⊢nSν(V)⊕mν.\mathcal L_n(V)\cong \bigoplus_{\nu\vdash n}\mathbb S_\nu(V)^{\oplus m_\nu}.Ln​(V)≅ν⊢n⨁​Sν​(V)⊕mν​.

Moreover, the multiplicities mνm_\numν​ are well understood. They can be computed using symmetric-group characters, or by counting certain standard Young tableaux.3

So we know how to decompose L(V)\mathcal L(V)L(V). The difficulty comes when we apply another Schur functor Sμ\mathbb S_\muSμ​ to it.

This leads us directly to plethysm.

Plethysm describes the composition of Schur functors. Given partitions μ\muμ and ν\nuν, we seek the decomposition

Sμ(Sν(V))≅⨁λ⊢∣μ∣∣ν∣Sλ(V)⊕pμ,νλ.\mathbb S_\mu\bigl(\mathbb S_\nu(V)\bigr) \cong \bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash|\mu||\nu|} \mathbb S_\lambda(V)^{\oplus p_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}}.Sμ​(Sν​(V))≅λ⊢∣μ∣∣ν∣⨁​Sλ​(V)⊕pμ,νλ​.

The nonnegative integers pμ,νλp_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}pμ,νλ​ are the plethysm coefficients. In the language of symmetric functions, writing sλs_\lambdasλ​ for the Schur function associated with Sλ\mathbb S_\lambdaSλ​, the same calculation is

sμ[sν]=∑λpμ,νλsλ.s_\mu[s_\nu]=\sum_\lambda p_{\mu,\nu}^{\lambda}s_\lambda.sμ​[sν​]=λ∑​pμ,νλ​sλ​.

For our problem, let Lien=∑ν⊢nmνsν\mathrm{Lie}_n=\sum_{\nu\vdash n}m_\nu s_\nuLien​=∑ν⊢n​mν​sν​ encode the degree-nnn piece of the free Lie algebra. The coefficients we seek are precisely those in the expansion:4

sμ[∑n≥1Lien]=∑λcλμsλ.s_\mu\left[\sum_{n\geq 1}\mathrm{Lie}_n\right] =\sum_\lambda c_{\lambda\mu}s_\lambda.sμ​[n≥1∑​Lien​]=λ∑​cλμ​sλ​.

Thus the representation-theoretic question reduces to computing plethysms of symmetric functions.

Unfortunately, plethysm is notoriously difficult.5 Littlewood-Richardson coefficients, which govern tensor products of Schur functors, admit an elegant positive combinatorial rule. No comparably general positive rule is known for plethysm coefficients.6 Even determining which irreducible representations occur in a plethysm can be subtle, and general computations quickly become prohibitively expensive as the partitions grow.

Roll up your sleeves​

Small examples of the coefficients cλμc_{\lambda\mu}cλμ​ can be computed by hand, but the calculations quickly become intractable. Sooner or later, one has to turn to a computer.

A confession: this was the first time in my mathematical career that I had found myself turning to a computer for help. My first attempts were brute force and, unsurprisingly, rather inefficient. They only produced coefficients through degree 5.

There are 18 nonempty partitions through degree 5, giving the 18×1818\times 1818×18 matrix below. Rows index the target partition λ\lambdaλ and columns the source partition μ\muμ.

Two features are immediately clear: the diagonal consists entirely of 1s, and everything above it is zero. Both are simple to prove directly. Since L1(V)=V\mathcal L_1(V)=VL1​(V)=V and there are no degree-zero terms, the lowest-degree part of Sμ(L(V))\mathbb S_\mu(\mathcal L(V))Sμ​(L(V)) is Sμ(V)\mathbb S_\mu(V)Sμ​(V) itself, in degree ∣μ∣|\mu|∣μ∣.

What interests us, then, is what lies strictly below the diagonal. Through degree 5, there is little to suggest a deeper pattern.

The key insight to improve on the naive brute-force approach was to recast the coefficients cλμc_{\lambda\mu}cλμ​ as weighted counts of solutions to certain combinatorial arrangements I called decomposition puzzles. The underlying combinatorics of these puzzles imposed clear restrictions on the kinds of assemblies that are valid, allowing us to significantly reduce the search space.

At the level of degrees, plethysm becomes multiplication and tensor product becomes addition. In the example above, the chosen pairing has degree 2×2+1×1=52\times 2+1\times 1=52×2+1×1=5. Swapping the Lie pieces gives 2×1+1×2=42\times 1+1\times 2=42×1+1×2=4, immediately ruling out that pairing for a degree-5 target.

This cheap check is the starting point of shape analysis.7 By grouping decompositions with the same part sizes, I could perform the search once per shape and reuse the resulting instructions across many calculations. I will give the details below.

This was the algorithm described in my 2017 paper. It extended the computation to degree 14: a 507×507507\times 507507×507 matrix containing 257,049 entries, compared with the original 324.

Visualizing these expanded coefficients revealed a striking block-stability pattern that immediately brought to mind Church, Ellenberg, and Farb's work on FI-modules.8 Blocks in one part of the matrix seemed to recur, with changes, farther down and to the right.

You can explore this observation yourself in the interactive figure below: toggle Show degree boundaries to separate the matrix into blocks of fixed source and target degree. Use the maximum-degree slider to compare the expanded table with the degree-5 calculation.

Before examining that pattern, let us look more closely at the puzzles that made a computation of this size possible.

Decomposition puzzles​

Return to the decomposition of the free Lie algebra, now indexing its irreducible summands individually:

L(V)≅⨁i≥1Sℓi(V).\mathcal L(V)\cong \bigoplus_{i\geq 1}\mathbb S_{\ell_i}(V).L(V)≅i≥1⨁​Sℓi​​(V).

The partitions ℓi\ell_iℓi​ label Lie pieces, with repeated summands listed separately. A μ\muμ-decomposition is a tuple D=(μ1,…,μk)D=(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k)D=(μ1​,…,μk​) of nonempty partitions satisfying ∑j∣μj∣=∣μ∣\sum_j|\mu_j|=|\mu|∑j​∣μj​∣=∣μ∣. Its iterated Littlewood-Richardson coefficient is

αμ(D)=[sμ](sμ1⋯sμk).\alpha_\mu(D) =[s_\mu]\bigl(s_{\mu_1}\cdots s_{\mu_k}\bigr).αμ​(D)=[sμ​](sμ1​​⋯sμk​​).

Retain only the decompositions with αμ(D)>0\alpha_\mu(D)>0αμ​(D)>0. For each one, choose a tuple I=(i1,…,ik)I=(i_1,\ldots,i_k)I=(i1​,…,ik​) of distinct Lie-piece indices and form the assembly

A(D,I)=∏j=1ksμj[sℓij],A(D,I)=\prod_{j=1}^k s_{\mu_j}[s_{\ell_{i_j}}],A(D,I)=j=1∏k​sμj​​[sℓij​​​],

where brackets denote plethysm. The multiplicity of a target partition λ\lambdaλ in this assembly is βλ(D,I)=[sλ]A(D,I)\beta_\lambda(D,I)=[s_\lambda]A(D,I)βλ​(D,I)=[sλ​]A(D,I).

A pairing in which λ\lambdaλ occurs is a solution to the puzzle, with weight αμ(D)βλ(D,I)\alpha_\mu(D)\beta_\lambda(D,I)αμ​(D)βλ​(D,I). Theorem 3.21 of the paper identifies cλμc_{\lambda\mu}cλμ​ with the sum over the set Σ(μ,λ)\Sigma(\mu,\lambda)Σ(μ,λ) of distinct solutions:9

cλμ=∑σ∈Σ(μ,λ)αμ(σ) βλ(σ).c_{\lambda\mu} =\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma(\mu,\lambda)} \alpha_\mu(\sigma)\,\beta_\lambda(\sigma).cλμ​=σ∈Σ(μ,λ)∑​αμ​(σ)βλ​(σ).

Shape analysis​

Enumerating every assembly would still require too many expensive plethysms. The useful restriction comes from homogeneity: an assembly has degree ∑j∣μj∣ ∣ℓij∣\sum_j|\mu_j|\,|\ell_{i_j}|∑j​∣μj​∣∣ℓij​​∣, so it can contribute to λ⊢d\lambda\vdash dλ⊢d only when that sum equals ddd.

This condition depends on the decomposition only through its shape

θ=(∣μ1∣,…,∣μk∣),\theta=(|\mu_1|,\ldots,|\mu_k|),θ=(∣μ1​∣,…,∣μk​∣),

with the pieces ordered by decreasing size. Writing ri=∣ℓi∣r_i=|\ell_i|ri​=∣ℓi​∣ for the Lie-piece degrees, the condition becomes

θ1ri1+⋯+θkrik=d.\theta_1r_{i_1}+\cdots+\theta_kr_{i_k}=d.θ1​ri1​​+⋯+θk​rik​​=d.

The shape also gives an upper bound on the degrees of the Lie pieces we need to consider.10 The algorithm searches this smaller collection for degree-compatible pairings and caches their indices. These instructions can then be reused by every decomposition of the same shape.

For θ=(2,1)\theta=(2,1)θ=(2,1) and target degree 5, the ten available Lie pieces give 90 ordered pairs. The bound restricts us to pieces of degree at most 3, leaving six pairs. The equation 2ri1+ri2=52r_{i_1}+r_{i_2}=52ri1​​+ri2​​=5 then leaves just two: the degree pairs (1,3)(1,3)(1,3) and (2,1)(2,1)(2,1).

The instruction count is not itself a coefficient. For μ=(2,1)\mu=(2,1)μ=(2,1) and D=((2),(1))D=((2),(1))D=((2),(1)), each of these two assemblies contributes one copy of the target (3,2)(3,2)(3,2). The decomposition D′=((1,1),(1))D'=((1,1),(1))D′=((1,1),(1)) contributes one further copy, so the full weighted sum is

c(3,2),(2,1)=3.c_{(3,2),(2,1)}=3.c(3,2),(2,1)​=3.

The algorithm and its computational range​

For a fixed target degree ddd, the implementation computes all coefficients with ∣λ∣=d|\lambda|=d∣λ∣=d simultaneously:

  1. Construct the instruction lookup for each shape and target degree.
  2. Enumerate the decompositions with nonzero Littlewood-Richardson multiplicity.
  3. Assemble the compatible instructions and accumulate their Schur coefficients with the appropriate weights and overcount correction.

The optimization does not eliminate plethysm; it avoids evaluating assemblies that cannot contribute.

The following comparison is from the experiments reported in the paper:

QuantityDirect baselineDecomposition-puzzle algorithm
Largest degree reached in the paper514
Entries in the resulting full matrix324257,049
Time to compute through degree 5119 seconds0.239 seconds

The paper's "over 750-fold" claim refers to the expanded number of matrix entries. The degree-5 timing comparison is a separate result: roughly 498 times faster in that experiment.

These are timings from the 2017 experiments, not benchmarks of current versions of Sage.11

Diagonal stabilization​

Return now to the pattern in the expanded matrix. The similarities between successive (m,d)(m,d)(m,d)- and (m+1,d+1)(m+1,d+1)(m+1,d+1)-blocks, where mmm and ddd are the source and target degrees, suggest adding a box to the first row of each indexing partition. Both degrees increase by one, while their difference stays fixed.

Write λ+r=(λ1+r,λ2,…)\lambda^{+r}=(\lambda_1+r,\lambda_2,\ldots)λ+r=(λ1​+r,λ2​,…) for adding rrr boxes to the first row. For a fixed pair (λ,μ)(\lambda,\mu)(λ,μ), consider the sequence

cλμ,cλ+1μ+1,cλ+2μ+2,…c_{\lambda\mu},\quad c_{\lambda^{+1}\mu^{+1}},\quad c_{\lambda^{+2}\mu^{+2}},\quad\ldotscλμ​,cλ+1μ+1​,cλ+2μ+2​,…

For example, the pair λ=(2,2,1)\lambda=(2,2,1)λ=(2,2,1), μ=(1,1)\mu=(1,1)μ=(1,1) gives the initial values 2,11,142,11,142,11,14, followed by the value 14 through r=9r=9r=9, the endpoint of the degree-14 computation. The figure allows this sequence to be compared with other pairs, including any pair selected in the matrix.

The computed plateaus suggest eventual constancy along these diagonals, rather than merely a similarity between finite blocks.

Conjecture 5.4 of the paper states that, for every fixed pair λ,μ\lambda,\muλ,μ, there exist constants N,CN,CN,C such that

cλ+rμ+r=Cfor all r≥N.c_{\lambda^{+r}\mu^{+r}}=C \qquad\text{for all }r\geq N.cλ+rμ+r​=Cfor all r≥N.

The finite computation motivates this statement but does not prove it or determine the onset of permanent stabilization.

Representation stability via PD-modules​

Chapter 5 of the thesis introduces PD-modules to describe this simultaneous growth. They organize representations indexed by two finite sets, with compatible maps that enlarge both sets by the same amount.12 Schur-Weyl duality identifies our coefficients as multiplicities in a PD-module built from the free Lie algebra.

The key condition is finite generation in rank: for each fixed difference between the two degrees, finitely many generators suffice under these diagonal structure maps. Theorem 5.5.3 shows that PD-modules with this property satisfy representation stability.

For the free Lie algebra, finite generation comes from the same degree constraint used by the algorithm. At fixed rank q=∣λ∣−∣μ∣q=|\lambda|-|\mu|q=∣λ∣−∣μ∣, it gives

q=∑j∣μj∣(∣ℓij∣−1).q=\sum_j|\mu_j|\bigl(|\ell_{i_j}|-1\bigr).q=j∑​∣μj​∣(∣ℓij​​∣−1).

Every Lie piece of degree greater than one contributes at least ∣μj∣|\mu_j|∣μj​∣ to this sum. The total source degree assigned to such pieces is therefore at most qqq. All unbounded growth must occur in the factor paired with the unique degree-one Lie piece, L1(V)=V\mathcal L_1(V)=VL1​(V)=V. This growth is encoded by the PD structure maps; the remaining assemblies have bounded degree and supply finitely many generators. Theorem 5.6.4 makes this argument precise.

It follows that our coefficients stabilize under simultaneous first-row augmentation. This is Theorem 5.6.5 of the thesis, proving the conjecture above.

The computation supplied evidence for the stability statement. The PD-module structure explains why it holds beyond the computed range.

Sources and reproducibility​

The article follows An efficient algorithm computing composition factors of T(V)⊗nT(V)^{\otimes n}T(V)⊗n, especially Sections 2.3, 3.4, 5, and 6. The proof of stability is in Chapter 5 of my thesis; Chapter 4 develops the algorithm and its visualizations. The original Sage implementation is on GitHub.

Data provenance. The figures use freshly reconstructed coefficients, not values extracted from images or a recovered archive of the original run. They were computed from the defining plethysm using exact arithmetic, independently of the paper's puzzle algorithm.13 The download includes the partition order, source reference, and a matrix checksum. All interactions use this precomputed table; no algebra is evaluated in the browser.

Footnotes​

    Lien=1n∑d∣nμMob(d) pdn/d,\mathrm{Lie}_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{d\mid n} \mu_{\mathrm{Mob}}(d)\,p_d^{n/d},Lien​=n1​d∣n∑​μMob​(d)pdn/d​,

    where μMob\mu_{\mathrm{Mob}}μMob​ is the Mobius function and pdp_dpd​ is the degree-ddd power-sum symmetric function. The infinite sum is taken in the degree-completed ring of symmetric functions; computing through any fixed degree requires only finitely many homogeneous terms. ↩

  8. Thomas Church, Jordan S. Ellenberg, and Benson Farb, FI-modules and stability for representations of symmetric groups, Duke Mathematical Journal 164, no. 9 (2015), pp. 1833-1910. ↩

  10. Order the shape parts decreasingly and the Lie-piece degrees r1,r2,…r_1,r_2,\ldotsr1​,r2​,… increasingly, counting multiplicities. Lemma 3.28 of the paper gives the upper bound

    φ(θ,d)=⌊d−∑j=1k−1θjrjθk⌋.\varphi(\theta,d)= \left\lfloor \frac{d-\sum_{j=1}^{k-1}\theta_jr_j}{\theta_k} \right\rfloor.φ(θ,d)=⌊θk​d−∑j=1k−1​θj​rj​​⌋.

    Pairing the largest shape parts with the smallest available degrees leaves the greatest possible allowance for the remaining piece. ↩
